clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by MTTP mutations that abolish microsomal triglyceride transfer protein activity, preventing assembly and secretion of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins.

Biochemical hallmark is near-absent low-density lipoprotein cholesterol with very low total cholesterol and triglycerides and undetectable chylomicrons, very-low-density lipoprotein and apolipoprotein B.
Presents in infancy with fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea, abdominal distension and failure to thrive.
Acanthocytosis (spiculated red cells) on the peripheral blood film is characteristic.
Progressive neurological disease resembling Friedreich ataxia, with spinocerebellar degeneration, loss of proprioception and vibration sense and areflexia, is driven largely by vitamin E deficiency.
An atypical pigmentary retinopathy causes progressive visual loss.
Coagulopathy arises from vitamin K malabsorption, and hepatic steatosis carries a risk of progression to fibrosis.
Early high-dose fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (especially vitamin E) with a diet low in long-chain fat can prevent or slow the neurological and retinal complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein resides in the endoplasmic reticulum of enterocytes and hepatocytes, where it transfers lipids onto nascent apolipoprotein B to assemble chylomicrons in the intestine and very-low-density lipoproteins in the liver. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MTTP abolish this activity, so apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins cannot be assembled or secreted. Dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins accumulate within enterocytes, producing fat malabsorption, while triglyceride accumulates in hepatocytes, producing steatosis. Circulating chylomicrons, very-low-density lipoprotein and low-density lipoprotein are effectively absent, and because vitamin E depends on lipoprotein transport its profound deficiency causes oxidative injury to neurons and the retina, manifesting as spinocerebellar degeneration and pigmentary retinopathy. Abnormal red-cell membrane lipid composition produces the characteristic acanthocytosis.
additionalDifferentials: Homozygous familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia (APOB mutations), which is clinically similar
Chylomicron retention disease (Anderson disease, SAR1B), with low but not absent apolipoprotein B and no acanthocytosis
Friedreich ataxia and ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency (TTPA mutations)
Coeliac disease and other causes of fat malabsorption in infancy
Other inherited and acquired causes of retinitis pigmentosa
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile showing very low total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein and triglycerides, with undetectable apolipoprotein B
Serum fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E and K), with vitamin E markedly reduced
Coagulation studies showing prolonged prothrombin time from vitamin K deficiency
MTTP gene molecular testing, with APOB testing to distinguish hypobetalipoproteinaemia
Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography, plus neurological examination and nerve conduction studies
Liver function tests and imaging for steatosis, with small-bowel biopsy showing lipid-laden vacuolated enterocytes
redFlags: Progressive ataxia, sensory neuropathy and visual loss indicating advancing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Bleeding tendency from vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy
Failure to thrive and severe malnutrition in infancy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and aggressive fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (especially vitamin E) together with dietary fat modification, the neurological and retinal complications can be largely prevented; late or untreated disease leads to progressive, disabling neurological and visual impairment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as coeliac disease or cystic fibrosis and delaying lipoprotein and genetic evaluation.
Under-treating with vitamin E, since much greater supplementation is needed than in simple deficiency because of the transport defect.
Confusing the condition with homozygous hypobetalipoproteinaemia, noting that parental lipid profiles are normal in abetalipoproteinaemia.
Overlooking acanthocytosis or attributing it to other causes.
Failing to monitor and correct coagulopathy before invasive procedures.
references: The Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (standard reference)
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease (standard reference)
